title: The Home Front
tagline: Ration books, victory gardens and the end of the Second World War.

locale.persona: a war-plant worker's family in Detroit

morningRoutine.detail: Millions of women worked in war industries: more than six million took war jobs.
Some foods needed ration stamps as well as money: red stamps for meat and butter, blue stamps for processed foods.

source.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States

morningRoutine.detail: By 1940, 83% of American homes owned a radio, the main way families followed the war.
Gasoline was rationed. The lowest-priority "A" sticker allowed about 3 to 4 gallons a week, so carpooling was common.

source.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States

morningRoutine.detail: Families grew vegetables in backyards and vacant lots; victory gardens grew about a third of the country's vegetables during the war.

technology.name: Household radio
technology.description: In 83% of homes by 1940 and 33 million households in 1945; families gathered around it for war news and the president's addresses.

technology.name: ENIAC
technology.description: The electronic computer was completed in 1945 and put to its first practical work on December 10.

technology.name: Buses and streetcars

futureVisions.prediction: A desk-sized "memex" will store a person's books and records and link them in trails of association.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: Vannevar Bush, "As We May Think", The Atlantic Monthly, July 1945
futureVisions.note: The memex was never built, but linked documents became hypertext and the World Wide Web.

futureVisions.prediction: Wholly new forms of encyclopedias will appear, ready-made with a mesh of associative trails running through them.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: Vannevar Bush, "As We May Think", July 1945
futureVisions.note: Online encyclopedias with hyperlinks are exactly this.

futureVisions.prediction: Satellites in a fixed orbit above the Earth could relay radio signals worldwide.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: Arthur C. Clarke, "Extra-Terrestrial Relays", Wireless World, October 1945
futureVisions.note: Geostationary communication satellites became standard from the 1960s.
